note: Proposed, not sealed. Found by chasing what looked like a trivial anomaly: `git fetch --prune --tags` surfaced a v0.11.1 tag that earlier fetches had not, and the first guess — that somebody had just pushed an old tag — was wrong. Earlier fetches used --prune without --tags, which only fetches tags reachable from the refs being fetched, and an orphaned tag is by definition unreachable. The tag had been there since 2026-08-25; what changed was the fetch flags. Chasing why it was unreachable is what turned up the rest.

decisions.question: What is the actual state of this repository's history, and how much of the published release record is reachable from master?
decisions.commitment: The history was REPLACED on 2026-08-25/26, not rewritten. `git merge-base v0.11.1 origin/master` returns nothing: the two sides share no common ancestor at all. Master is rooted at 7f91b12 (2026-08-25 19:27, 'Plumb --matcher through nestor decision check (#212)') and was 169 commits when this was written; the other side is 832 and cannot grow. Nineteen release tags (v0.2.0 through v0.11.1) are not ancestors of master, and `git for-each-ref --contains b44cc4f` returns only the tag itself — those commits are held alive by their tags and by nothing else. The tags from v0.12.0 onward are on the mainline and that set grows with every release. CHANGELOG.md presents every release as one continuous story from 0.2.0, so the nineteen entries covering 0.2.0 through 0.11.1 describe commits that are not in this repository's mainline — a fixed nineteen against a denominator that climbs. The entry for 0.12.0 links `compare/v0.11.1...v0.12.0`, a comparison across two unrelated histories; run locally that diff is 67 files changed, 13718 insertions.
decisions.why: Two of the counts above are point-in-time and are written that way on purpose. Between drafting this decision and rebasing it onto master, PR #270 merged and 0.18.1 was cut: master went 169 -> 174 commits, mainline tags 9 -> 10, CHANGELOG entries 29 -> 30. That is decision 0231's thesis arriving on 0231's successor within hours, which is worth stating rather than quietly correcting. The durable facts are the ones the argument rests on and none of them moved: no merge-base, nineteen orphaned tags, 832 commits on a side that cannot grow, root 7f91b12. Recorded because the tree does not say it anywhere. Grepped for 'greenfield', 'fresh history', 'new root' and 're-land' across docs/, IDEAS.md, README.md and docs/agent-log.md: nothing. The word 'greenfield' appears once, in docs/progress-catalog/README.md, referring to other trees. So the single largest fact about this repository's history is undocumented inside it, and the only way to find it is to notice that a tag will not fetch. A reader running `git log` sees 169 commits and a CHANGELOG asserting 29 releases back to 0.2.0, and has no way to reconcile the two. For a project whose claim is that a record is auditable and its chain joins, an undocumented discontinuity in its own release history is the finding that most needs writing down rather than least.

decisions.question: Is this a defect to repair, or a fact to document?
decisions.commitment: A fact to document. Nothing here is proposed as a repair: not grafting the histories, not rewriting CHANGELOG.md, not deleting or retargeting the nineteen tags. The reasons the replacement happened are operator knowledge and are not derivable from the tree, so a session cannot supply them and should not invent them. What is added is a section in docs/build-record.md, under the heading that already exists for exactly this — 'What this record does not establish' — and a line in docs/releasing.md recording that the pre-0.12.0 tags are load-bearing.
decisions.why: Every repair is worse than the disclosure. Grafting with a replace-ref or a graft commit invents an ancestry that did not happen, in a repository arguing that provenance should be checkable. Rewriting CHANGELOG.md to start at 0.12.0 would delete the record of nine published PyPI versions; a version on PyPI can never be reused, so the changelog is the only place several releases are described at all. Retargeting the tags would move published release markers off the commits that were actually released. The honest move in each case is the same one the codebase already makes elsewhere: say what is true, say what cannot be seen from here, and leave the operator's decision to the operator.

decisions.question: What protects the nineteen orphaned tags, and what happens if one is deleted?
decisions.commitment: Nothing protects them today, and docs/releasing.md now says so. Those tags are the sole refs keeping 832 commits reachable. Deleting one on the remote makes its commits unreferenced; a fresh clone would not carry them, and local garbage collection eventually reclaims them. GitHub retains unreachable objects for a while and this is not a same-day loss, but it is a one-command, unrecoverable-in-principle loss of published-release provenance, and no gate or note stands between an operator and it. Not proposed here: a test asserting the tag set, or branch/tag protection rules. Both are real options and both are operator decisions about a remote's configuration rather than code.
decisions.why: The seat rule this session was handed reads: no work is lost until `git stash list` and the reflog agree it is, and a `git fetch` without `--prune` invents dead branches. This is the same class one level up — a repository can be missing most of its own history while every ordinary command reports success. `git log` is clean, `git describe` resolves, CI is green, the version numbers increment correctly, and none of that touches the 832 commits hanging off nineteen tags. Writing the dependency down is the cheapest thing that makes it visible before somebody tidies up a tag list.
